title: Baddi — wanting, and a cup of coffee
goal: Say what you want and don't want, order coffee and tea properly, and understand why بَدِّي is not a verb even though it means one.
bekal: attach the eight possessive endings to بَدّ
order a drink with the right amount of sugar
ask for something politely without sounding bossy

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِالْقَهْوِة
dialogs.intro: An old coffee house in Damascus, midday. Budi comes in with Samer, and a waiter comes over to the table.

lines.speaker: اَلْجَرْسُون:
lines.id: Welcome. What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.text: يَعْنِي سُكَّر شْوَي كْتِير. مِش سَادَة.
lines.baca: ya‘ni sikkar shway ktiir. mish saade.
lines.id: It means very little sugar. Not completely without.
lines.literal: meaning sugar little much. not plain.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK, I'll have a medium-sweet one.

lines.speaker: اَلْجَرْسُون:
lines.id: Fine. Would you like something with it?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.id: Bring us some water too, please.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Samer, don't you want to eat something?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.id: No, I'm full. I ate a little while ago.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: w ana juu‘aan. baddi shi hilu.
lines.id: I'm hungry. I want something sweet.
lines.literal: and I hungry. want-my something sweet.

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.id: Try the baklava. It's the best thing here.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK. A plate of baklava, please.

notes: **The word بَدِّي is not a verb, and that's not just hair-splitting.** It's really بَدّ plus the possessive endings you learned in unit 4 — the same pattern as عِنْدِي. That's why it has no past form, can't take the prefix b-, and is negated with مَا — for example مَا بَدِّي.

**After بَدِّي, the verb loses its b- prefix.** "I drink" is بِشْرَب, but "I want to drink" is بَدِّي إِشْرَب — no b. The same rule applies after لَازِم and مُمْكِن in unit 15, and after رَح in unit 14. Remember the rule now, and the next three units get easy.
**If what you want is a thing, not an action, just name the thing.** The phrase بَدِّي قَهْوِة is complete and correct. No verb needed at all, just like English "I want coffee".

**Arabic coffee comes with a sugar level you have to name.** There are four options: سَادَة (no sugar at all), عَ الرِّيحَة (very little), وَسَط (medium) and حِلْوِة (sweet). If you say nothing, you'll get وَسَط — always a safe choice.
**The phrase لَو سَمَحْت is the safest "please".** Literally "if you permit". The form مِن فَضْلَك is also correct but a little more formal. To a woman both change: لَو سَمَحْتِي and مِن فَضْلِك.

**The phrase صَحْتَين is said to someone who is eating or about to eat.** Literally "two healths". The reply is عَ قَلْبَك ("on your heart") or, if you're eating together, تِسْلَم إِيدَيْك to whoever cooked.

grammars.title: The eight forms of بَدّ
after: ⚠️ Watch out for a dangerous pair: **بَدَّك** (you, man) and **بَدِّك** (you, woman). Just one vowel apart, exactly like كِيفَك and كِيفِك in unit 1. This pattern runs through all of Levantine Arabic.
In Jordan and Palestine the form is slightly different: بِدِّي *biddi*, with i instead of a. Both are understood everywhere; pick either one, as long as you're consistent.

grammars.title: The bare verb after بَدِّي
body: The verb form that follows بَدِّي is called the bare form — without the b- prefix. It's the basic form you'll use again after رَح، لَازِم، مُمْكِن، and فِيني. This table uses the verb شِرِب (to drink).
after: There really is just one rule: **drop the b at the front.** The form بِشْرَب becomes إِشْرَب · بْتِشْرَب becomes تِشْرَب · بْيِشْرَب becomes يِشْرَب. Once you know the b- forms from unit 8, you automatically know these.
⚠️ The number-one mistake at this point is saying بَدِّي بِشْرَب with the b still attached. It sounds wrong right away — a bit like "I want to drinks" in English.

blocks.text: Coffee called قَهْوِة with nothing else added always means Arabic coffee boiled with its grounds, not filter coffee. If you want European-style coffee, name it: كَابُتْشِينُو، إِسْبْرِيسُو، أَمِيرِيكَانُو. All of these are understood across the Levant.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Coffee in the Levant is more than a drink
items: Turning down coffee offered by a host is like turning down their hospitality. If you really can't, decline with a blessing: اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك، بَسّ لِسَّا شَارِب.
Bitter coffee with no sugar (سَادَة) has a special meaning at funerals and marriage proposals. In an ordinary café it's just a taste preference, so don't worry about ordering it.
The phrases تْفَضَّل and صَحْتَين apply to drinks too, not just food. If someone hands you a glass, the safe reply is always يِسْلَمُوا.

blocks.text: The form جِيبْلِي sounds like an order if you translate it literally, but in cafés and restaurants it's completely normal and not rude — as long as it comes with لَو سَمَحْت. Used with someone who isn't serving you, though, it sounds impolite.

blocks.title: Three adjectives for how you feel that you'll use a lot
items: The word جُوعَان *juu‘aan* means hungry, and شَبْعَان *shab‘aan* means full. The feminine forms are جُوعَانِة and شَبْعَانِة.
The word عَطْشَان *‘aṭshaan* means thirsty, and تَعْبَان *ta‘baan* means tired. Both follow the same pattern.
⚠️ All of these are **adjectives**, not verbs — so their negative is مِش, not مَا — for example أَنَا مِش جُوعَان.
What would you (f) like to drink?
We don't want to eat now.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of بَدّ.
Drop the b- prefix to get the right form after بَدِّي.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: بَدِّي قَهْوِة سَادَة. — شُو بَدِّك تِشْرْبِي؟ — مَا بَدْنَا نَاكُل هَلَّق. — لَو سَمَحْت، كُبَّايِة مَي. — بَدُّو يْنَام. — أَنَا جُوعَان كْتِير.
بَدِّي — بَدَّك — بَدُّو — بَدْنَا — بَدْكُن — بَدِّك
بَدِّي إِشْرَب مَي — بَدَّك تَاكُل شِي؟ — بَدُّو يْنَام هَلَّق — بَدْنَا نْرُوح عَ السُّوق — بَدَّا تِدْرُس عَرَبِي — بَدْهُن يِجُوا بُكْرَا
بَدِّي قَهْوِة سَادَة. — شُو بَدَّك تِشْرَب؟ — جِيبْلِي مَي لَو سَمَحْت. — أَنَا جُوعَان كْتِير. — مَا بَدِّي شِي شُكْرًا. — بَدِّي شِي حِلُو.
wave: Order coffee three times in your head today — once سَادَة, once وَسَط, once حِلْوِة — and add لَو سَمَحْت to every sentence.
